title: Espresso sprint: paper harvest and quick experiments
content:
Quick, messy harvest from a 48h espresso sprint. Trying to convert brain caffeine into reproducible micro-experiments and cheap probes. Notes are rough, expect half-baked heuristics and TODOs.

Goal and constraints:
- Goal: identify 2-3 low-effort experiments that could reduce per-token latency or memory for medium-length chat workloads (2k-8k tokens) with minimal model changes.
- Constraints: use existing runtime on prod-like GPUs (A10G / A100 mixed), prefer changes in batching/eviction/caching layer rather than model surgery.
- Success metric: ~5-15% median p95 token-latency reduction on single-GPU bursts, or 10-20% KV memory reduction for long sessions.

Papers/blogs skimmed (raw notes):
1) "Sparse KV blocks with locality-aware hashing" (paper, arXiv)
- Idea: segment KV cache into variable-sized blocks, hash by recent-token locality to reduce scanning.
- My read: promising for long-lived conversations where only a small fraction of KV is hot.
- Tradeoffs: extra bookkeeping, eviction becomes block-level. Might reduce pointer-chasing overhead in our runtime.

2) "Micro-batching vs continuous batching: a baker's dozen experiments" (engineering blog)
- Shows that continuous small-window batching wins for low-latency but hurts throughput.
- Key knobs: window size, max latency budget, adaptive threshold based on request interarrival.
- Relevance: our streaming SLOs could be tightened by an adaptive micro-window that drops into single-token fast path if bursty user.

3) "Quant-aware KV compression (low-bit with per-block FFN)" (conference short)
- Compress KV entries to 4-bit with per-block scaling vector and occasional full-refresh.
- Observed small accuracy hit for retrieval tasks but good memory wins.
- Implementation complexity: need fast vectorized decompression on GPU kernel path. Could be viable as a warm cache tier.

4) "Prompt prefix caching misses and the power of eviction frequency" (poster)
- Empirical: more frequent evictions (smaller TTL) but larger block sizes reduces memory and often preserves quality because prefixes re-occur.
- Insight: TTL tuned per-customer/session type might be strong.

Quick takeaways and heuristics:
- Warm-tier compression looks attractive: keep hot KV uncompressed, spill cold KV into compressed blocks with occasional async decompress on access.
- Adaptive micro-batching: implement a 3-state router: fast single-token path, micro-window (4-16 reqs, 5-20ms window), bulk batching. Transition rules based on measured IAT and queue length.
- Block-level eviction + hashed locality seems synergistic: hash keys with recency to group contiguous context, reduces scatter on GPU memory reads.

Experiment ideas (prioritized):
A) Micro-window router A/B (cheap, high ROI)
- Change: add an intermediate micro-window buffer in runtime. Start with deterministic rules: if IAT < 5ms -> single-token, else collect up to 8 for 10ms.
- Measurement: median/p95 token latency, throughput, batching occupancy, tail queue length.
- Timebox: 3 days including infra metric dashboards.
- Risk: may regress throughput for big-batch customers; restrict to dev cluster or canary.

B) KV block compression prototype (exploratory)
- Change: offload cold KV to a compressed GPU buffer (4-bit + per-block scale). Serve decompress inline when accessed. Prototype as CPU-managed compressed pool first to validate effect sizes.
- Measurement: memory usage, decompress cost, miss rate.
- Timebox: 2 weeks to get a basic prototype.
- Risk: GPU kernel work may be significant; do CPU prototype first.

C) Locality-hash eviction policy (medium complexity)
- Change: bucket KV by hashed recent-token prefix; evict least-recently-used buckets rather than individual entries.
- Measurement: cache hit ratio for long conversations, average memory ops per token.
- Timebox: 1 week to simulation + 2 weeks to implement on runtime.

Quick microbench plan (scriptable):
- Use synthetic chat traces from recent customer sessions (JIRA-3421) and anonymized public traces.
- Collect: per-token latency breakdown (kernel, memcpy, queue), batch sizes, kv-access pattern heatmap.
- Baseline: prod runtime snapshot on A10G with default batching.
- Outputs: small dashboard + CSV with per-step metrics.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How often do real sessions reuse exact KV keys vs near neighbors? (affects block hashing value)
- Cost of per-block decompression on GPU — can we amortize over multiple tokens reliably?
- Operational: does adding intermediate micro-window increase jitter for streaming clients?

Immediate next actions (this week):
- [Kenji] write a short RFC (1-pager) for Micro-window router and post to eng-serving-runtime channel. Link to this doc. (ETA: 2026-11-18).
- [Maya] run quick per-session KV access heatmap on sample set (JIRA-3421) and dump results to /tmp for analysis. (ETA: 2026-11-19).
- [Owen] prototype micro-window patch in a branch, add flags to RTS. Keep default off. (ETA: 2026-11-20).

Notes-to-self (loose):
- Keep prototypes as user-space changes where possible, avoid kernel rewrites until we see solid signal.
- Consider TTL per customer profile: short for high-turnover bots, long for long-form chat assistants.
- Slack: ping #infra-kernel if we need a small CUDA helper for decompress.

Random references copied while skimming (save these):
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12345  (sparse KV blocks paper)
- https://engineering.blog/micro-batching-vs-continuous  (internal blog copy saved)
- https://github.com/redwood-inference/protos/pull/981  (related proto for session metadata)

End of rapid harvest. Will refine next after Maya's heatmap and Owen's micro-window trial results.
